segments.voice: Yesterday, the Kama Sutra's ethics chapter defined the three aims, and kama as fitting joy with the whole self there. Today, what happens when the three collide.

Saturday, and it's triple-booked. A paid shift you picked up. A promise to help a cousin move apartments. A party you've been looking forward to for weeks. The calendar app shows three overlapping blocks, and something has to give. Vatsyayana, writing about the aims of life, saw this kind of Saturday coming, and he left a rule for it.
screen: `A SHIFT. A PROMISE. A PARTY.` → `THREE BLOCKS, ONE SATURDAY.` → `SOMETHING HAS TO GIVE.`

segments.voice: When the three aims pull against each other, he says, the earlier one outweighs the later. Dharma over artha. Artha over kama. So a book named for pleasure, in its own ethics chapter, puts pleasure third. Notice the condition, though. It's a rule for when they collide, not an order to drop the later aims. Yesterday the same chapter gave kama its own definition and its own place. And the ladder bends. For a king, Vatsyayana says, artha should come first, because people's livelihood depends on it. That's the Arthashastra's verdict from a few days ago, back again, but only for the job of ruling. Where you stand changes the order. So, one way to read that Saturday through this chapter: when you can't have all three, start with what's right, like the promise; then what keeps you going, like the shift; then what you enjoy. And if other people's living depends on your work, that can move up. The question the chapter keeps asking isn't how to get more of any one aim. It's how all three fit in one life without one swallowing the rest.
screen: `WHEN THEY CLASH: EARLIER OUTWEIGHS LATER.` · `DHARMA, THEN ARTHA, THEN KAMA.` · `NOT A RULE TO DROP THE LATER AIMS.` · `FOR A KING, ARTHA FIRST.` · then, large: `EVEN HERE, PLEASURE COMES THIRD.`

segments.voice: Think of one clash coming up in your own week: two things wanting the same hour. Name what you'd most want, the one thing in the way, and one small step that honors the higher aim without throwing the other away. Then breathe slowly, and let the plan settle.
The Kama Sutra's ethics chapter: when the aims collide, dharma, then artha, then kama, with artha first for a king.

howItsDone: Hindu teachers often explain the purusharthas, the aims of life, as a balance in which dharma guides the others; the Kama Sutra's opening is one classic place where their order in a conflict is set out.
